name: Japanese gidayū-bushi (Bunraku narration)
lineage: Japanese gidayū-bushi sung-and-spoken narration tradition, the canonical narrative-vocal style of ningyō jōruri Bunraku puppet-theater. Named after the founding seventeenth-century narrator Takemoto Gidayū (1651-1714), who codified the style at the Takemoto-za puppet-theater in Osaka beginning in 1684 and whose canonical works (such as the Sonezaki Shinjū love-suicide play, 1703, written by his collaborator Chikamatsu Monzaemon) established the genre's core repertoire. Bunraku-as-form. Performance configuration: a single tayū (narrator) sits on a raised platform stage-right, holding the maruhon scroll-text and shifting between speaking voices for multiple characters and the omniscient narrator, while a shamisen player (three-string plucked lute, specifically the heavy-bodied futozao shamisen reserved for jōruri) sits beside providing accompaniment that is structurally inseparable from the vocal narration — a single composition of tayū-and-shamisen voice. The narrative style spans a vast emotional and acoustic range: from quiet bedchamber confidence to climactic suicide-scene wails, from comedic banter to mortal-injury death-rattle, with the tayū employing a striking range of voice-types and registers. Repertoire genealogically connected to the older Heike-monogatari biwa-narrative and to the medieval Buddhist sermon-chant traditions. Twentieth-century canonical tayū include Toyotake Yamashiro-no-Shōjō, Takemoto Tsudayū, and contemporary masters of the National Bunraku Theatre lineage. Distinguished from gagaku court music by gidayū's narrative-theatrical (vs ceremonial-orchestral) functional framework; distinguished from kabuki nagauta by jōruri's puppet-theater accompaniment context.
